title: Singapore Had Nothing. Now It's Richer Than America.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: On the ninth of August 1965, a prime minister sat in front of television cameras and broke down in tears.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: His country had just been thrown out of the nation it had joined only two years earlier. It was now on its own.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And on paper, it had almost no chance.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It was a small island, smaller than the city of London. No oil. No gold. No farmland. Not even enough fresh water for its own people.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Nearly one in ten workers had no job. Many families lived in crowded wooden slums that could burn down in an afternoon.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The average person earned around five hundred dollars a year. About the same as Mexico or South Africa at the time.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That country was Singapore.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Now look at it today. In 2026, the average Singaporean produces more than a hundred and seven thousand dollars a year.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That is more than the average American. More than the British, the French and the Germans. One of the highest figures on Earth.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It has one of the busiest ports in the world, one of the cleanest governments in the world, and most families own their own home.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So how does a swamp with nothing go from five hundred dollars to more than a hundred thousand in one lifetime?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It wasn't oil. It wasn't luck. And it definitely wasn't easy.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: To understand it, we have to go back to the moment someone first noticed this little island was in exactly the right place.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Look at a map of Asia.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Between India and China there is a narrow strip of sea called the Strait of Malacca.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Every ship from China to India passed through one narrow strait.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And right at the bottom of that strait, at the very tip of the Malay Peninsula, sits one small island.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1819, a British official named Stamford Raffles landed there and set up a trading post for the British East India Company.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: His idea was simple. Make it a free port. No taxes on trade. Let every ship stop, buy, sell and move on.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It worked. Merchants came from China, India, the Malay world, the Middle East and Europe.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Within decades, Singapore became one of the great trading hubs of the British empire.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But here's the catch. Singapore didn't make much. It moved other people's goods.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It bought rubber and tin from the Malayan mainland and sold them on. It earned a living as a middleman.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And the British army and navy based there spent a lot of money and gave a lot of jobs.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the 1950s, that model was running out of road. The population had exploded, and there weren't nearly enough jobs or homes.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1959, around two hundred thousand people were unemployed. That's roughly one in seven people on the whole island.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Two hundred thousand unemployed. Hundreds of thousands more in squatter huts.

segments.speaker: MOTHER_1
segments.text: Why are we sleeping in shifts again?

segments.speaker: FATHER_1
segments.text: Because there are eleven of us and one room.

segments.speaker: MOTHER_1
segments.text: Eleven people. One room. Singapore in 1959.

segments.speaker: FATHER_1
segments.text: Then we sleep in very short shifts.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That same year, 1959, Singapore won the right to govern itself. The new government, led by Lee Kuan Yew, inherited every one of those problems.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In May 1961, a fire swept through the wooden village of Bukit Ho Swee. Around sixteen thousand people lost their homes in a single day.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The Housing and Development Board had been set up just a year earlier. It had the families rehoused in new concrete flats within about nine months.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Remember that. It's the first clue to how this country works.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But the government knew housing alone wouldn't fix anything. Singapore needed jobs, and it believed it couldn't survive as a tiny island on its own.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So in 1963, Singapore joined its neighbours to form a new country: Malaysia.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A big market. A big hinterland. Safety in numbers.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It lasted less than two years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: From the start, the marriage was unhappy.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore's leaders and the leaders in Kuala Lumpur disagreed about politics, about money, and above all about how a country of many races should be run.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1964, riots between communities broke out in Singapore, and people were killed.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Malaysia's prime minister decided the only way to avoid more bloodshed was to cut Singapore loose.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The deal was negotiated in secret. On the morning of the ninth of August 1965, it was announced on the radio.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore was out.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Lee Kuan Yew faced the cameras. He was fighting back tears.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: He had spent years arguing that Singapore could not survive alone. Now it had to.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Think about what was lost overnight. The big market of the Malaysian mainland was now a foreign country, with its own tariffs.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Next door, Indonesia was in an undeclared conflict with Malaysia, and trade with Singapore had been badly disrupted.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The island imported most of its food. It drew much of its water through pipes from across the border, from the very neighbour that had just shown it the door.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And then, two years later, came the second blow.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Britain was running short of money and pulling back from Asia. In 1967 it announced it would close its bases east of Suez. Soon after, it brought the deadline forward to 1971.

segments.speaker: BRIT_OFF
segments.text: I'm afraid we're leaving.

segments.speaker: SG_CLERK
segments.text: When?

segments.speaker: BRIT_OFF
segments.text: 1971. The British are leaving.

segments.speaker: SG_CLERK
segments.text: How many jobs is that?

segments.speaker: BRIT_OFF
segments.text: About thirty thousand jobs. A fifth of the economy.

segments.speaker: SG_CLERK
segments.text: And how much of the economy?

segments.speaker: BRIT_OFF
segments.text: Roughly a fifth.

segments.speaker: SG_CLERK
segments.text: No hinterland. No resources. No big market. And now, no army base.

segments.speaker: BRIT_OFF
segments.text: Good luck.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That's not an exaggeration. The British military accounted for about a fifth of Singapore's economy and more than thirty thousand jobs.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: No hinterland. No resources. A shaky water supply. And the biggest employer packing its bags.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Most experts at the time would not have bet on Singapore.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Quick pause. If you're enjoying this, subscribe to Farthing Explains. It's free, and it takes up even less space than Singapore.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Start with the scariest problem: water.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore gets plenty of rain, but it's too small to store much of it. So it relied on pipes from the Malaysian state of Johor.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Under a deal signed in 1962, Singapore can draw up to 250 million gallons a day from the Johor River, at a price of three Malaysian cents per thousand gallons.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That price has not changed since 1962. The deal runs until 2061. And Johor still supplies around forty percent of Singapore's water.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But every Singaporean leader knew that a country whose taps can be turned off by a neighbour is not fully free.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So Singapore spent decades building what it calls its four national taps: rain caught in reservoirs, water from Johor, seawater turned fresh, and the strangest one of all.

segments.speaker: DAUGHTER
segments.text: Dad, where does this water come from?

segments.speaker: FATHER_2
segments.text: Some of it comes from the sewers.

segments.speaker: DAUGHTER
segments.text: I'm not thirsty anymore.

segments.speaker: FATHER_2
segments.text: Recycled. Filtered. Cleaned to drinking-water standards.

segments.speaker: DAUGHTER
segments.text: They gave toilet water a brand name?

segments.speaker: FATHER_2
segments.text: And it works.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It really does. Recycled water called NEWater now meets up to forty percent of Singapore's demand. Most goes to factories, but some is topped up into the reservoirs.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Next, homes.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Remember that fire at Bukit Ho Swee? The Housing and Development Board kept building at that speed, block after block, for decades.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Then came the clever part. The government didn't want Singaporeans to rent. It wanted them to own.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Families could buy their flat using money from their own pension fund.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Every worker had to save part of their wages in that fund, and their employer added more. That gave the country a mountain of savings to invest, and gave families a stake in the country's future.

segments.speaker: SON
segments.text: Mum, is this flat really ours?

segments.speaker: MOTHER_2
segments.text: Ours, and the bank's, and your father's pension's.

segments.speaker: SON
segments.text: Over eighty percent of Singaporeans own their home. Using their own pension savings.

segments.speaker: MOTHER_2
segments.text: It's ours.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Today more than eighty percent of Singaporeans live in public housing, and the vast majority of those flats are owned by the families living in them.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And third: the iron rules.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore decided corruption would be treated as a serious crime, not a cost of doing business. A tough anti-corruption law was passed in 1960, and an independent bureau was given real teeth.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Today Transparency International ranks Singapore the third least corrupt country in the world.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It also tamed its labour disputes. New laws in the late 1960s limited strikes, and by the late 1970s strikes had almost disappeared.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Critics say these rules came with a price, and we'll get to that. But for a foreign company deciding where to build a factory, the message was clear.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The rules are the rules. No exceptions. No cash in the envelope.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Most poor countries in the 1960s were suspicious of big foreign companies. They put up tariffs, protected local firms and tried to make everything at home.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Argentina did exactly that, as we saw in our last episode.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore did the opposite. It went looking for the biggest companies in the world and asked them to come.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The job went to the Economic Development Board, set up in 1961 on the advice of a Dutch economist, Albert Winsemius.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Its first big project was a swamp in the west of the island called Jurong. Crocodiles in the creeks. Almost nothing else.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The government drained it, flattened hills, laid roads and built an industrial estate before there were any tenants. Critics called it Goh's Folly, after the finance minister.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: At first, almost nobody came. Goh Keng Swee flew around the world begging.

segments.speaker: EXEC
segments.text: So why should I build my factory here?

segments.speaker: EDB_OFF
segments.text: Our workers speak English. The land is ready. Power and water are connected.

segments.speaker: EXEC
segments.text: And taxes?

segments.speaker: EDB_OFF
segments.text: Up to ninety percent off your profits tax. For ten years.

segments.speaker: EXEC
segments.text: And bribes?

segments.speaker: EDB_OFF
segments.text: Try one and you'll go to jail.

segments.speaker: EXEC
segments.text: Where do I sign?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Tax holidays. Ready land. English-speaking workers. The pitch was real.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: From 1968, the big names started to arrive. National Semiconductor came first, and Texas Instruments, Hewlett-Packard and General Electric followed.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the end of the 1960s, Jurong had 181 factories in production. Goh's Folly wasn't a folly anymore.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The British bases were turned into something useful too. Their land was converted for business, and their naval dockyards became commercial shipyards.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Basic goods. Electronics. Finance. Services. Each decade, one rung higher.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the 1980s, Singapore was the world's leading producer of hard disk drives.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: From 1965 to the mid-1980s, the economy grew by around ten percent a year.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The port never stopped. In 2025, the second busiest container port on earth.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And from the 1970s, banks followed the ships. Singapore turned itself into a financial centre for the whole region.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The result? Around five hundred dollars per person in 1965. Around thirteen thousand by 1990. Around fifty-six thousand by 2015. More than a hundred and seven thousand today.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So is Singapore a paradise? Ask Singaporeans, and many will tell you it's more complicated.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Start with the cost of living. Land is scarce, so almost everything that needs space is expensive.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Want a car? Before you even buy one, you need a government permit just to own it for ten years.

visual.title: CERTIFICATE OF ENTITLEMENT
visual.sub: Required to own a car. Valid 10 years.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In October 2026, the permit for a small car cost about 132,000 Singapore dollars. That's the permit. Not the car.

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: How much for this little car?

segments.speaker: SALESMAN
segments.text: The car, or the right to drive the car?

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: There's a difference?

segments.speaker: SALESMAN
segments.text: A hundred and thirty thousand dollars. Just for the right to drive.

segments.speaker: CUSTOMER
segments.text: I'll take the bus.

segments.speaker: SALESMAN
segments.text: Everyone says that. The bus is very good.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The work is intense too. In 2015, Singaporeans worked around 2,300 hours a year, far more than most people in Europe.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The wealth isn't spread evenly. Inequality is high for a rich country, and the economy depends heavily on foreign workers, many of them on low wages.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: One party. Every election. Since 1959.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Critics, including press-freedom groups, say the media and the opposition have operated under tight limits for decades.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Supporters say that same stability is exactly what made the wealth possible.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Remember Argentina, where every new government undid the last one's work? Singapore is close to the opposite.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: There's one more risk. A country that lives by trade can also be hurt by trade. When the world economy stumbles, Singapore feels it fast.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That's the bargain. Extraordinary wealth and order, paid for with high costs, hard work and a lot of trust in the people in charge.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So let's put it together.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A swamp in the right place. A free port. A fire that taught the government to build fast. A divorce nobody wanted. An army that packed up and left.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So how did a country with nothing get richer than America? Most economists point to a few things working together.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: First, it turned its weakness into a sales pitch. With no natural resources to fight over, it sold the one thing it could control: being the easiest, safest, cleanest place in Asia to do business.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Second, it opened its doors when most poor countries were closing theirs. Instead of protecting weak local firms, it brought in the world's best companies and learned from them.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Third, it kept the rules stable. Low corruption, plans that lasted decades, and money that people trusted.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And fourth, it gave ordinary people a stake. Compulsory savings and home ownership meant most families owned a piece of the country's success.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Singapore's own leaders will tell you there's a fifth ingredient: paranoia. A small country that never feels safe never stops planning.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: That's the real contrast with Argentina. Argentina was born rich and kept losing trust. Singapore was born poor and built trust brick by brick.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Natural wealth can make you rich for a while. Trust, it turns out, compounds.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If you made it this far, thank you. Subscribe to Farthing Explains for more stories about how money makes and breaks countries.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Next time: a small island that makes almost all of the world's most advanced computer chips, and why that makes it one of the most valuable, and most nervous, places on Earth. See you there.
